overview.tagline: Walk two indices through the array instead of using nested loops.
whenToUse: The array or string is sorted, or order doesn't block a single pass.
You're searching for a pair, a window, or a partition.
A brute force would be O(n²) with nested loops over the same array.
You want to solve it with O(1) extra space.
overview.keyIdea: Place two pointers, often at both ends or one chasing the other, and move them based on a comparison, so each element is visited at most once. That collapses O(n²) into a single O(n) pass.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) time, O(1) space

overview.tagline: Slide a window across the array and update the answer as it grows and shrinks, instead of recomputing it from scratch.
whenToUse: You need the best, longest, or shortest contiguous subarray or substring.
Recomputing each window from scratch would be O(n·k) or O(n²).
The window can extend on the right and shrink on the left based on a condition.
You're tracking a running sum, count, or set over a contiguous range.
overview.keyIdea: Keep a window [L, R]. Expand R to take in new elements; when the window breaks a constraint (or to hold a fixed size), advance L. Each element enters and leaves the window once, so the whole sweep is O(n).
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) time, O(1) or O(k) space

lessons.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

overview.tagline: Halve the search space every step by exploiting sorted order.
whenToUse: The data is sorted, or the answer is monotonic, true then false.
You're searching for a value, a boundary, or a threshold.
A linear scan would be O(n) and you want O(log n).
You can decide which half to keep after looking at the middle.
overview.keyIdea: Track a range [lo, hi]. Look at the middle: if it's the target you're done; otherwise the comparison tells you which half can't hold the answer, so discard it. Each step throws away half of what remains, so it runs in O(log n).
overview.complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space

lessons.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

overview.tagline: Rearrange the array into order by repeatedly comparing and swapping elements.
whenToUse: You need data in order, or sorting unlocks a simpler next step (two pointers, binary search).
The input is small enough that O(n^2) is fine, or you're learning how ordering works.
You want an in-place rearrangement with O(1) extra space.
You need a stable order: insertion and bubble keep equal elements in their original sequence.
overview.keyIdea: Each algorithm grows a sorted region one element at a time. Bubble floats the largest to the end each pass; selection picks the smallest and places it; insertion slides each new value back into the sorted prefix.
overview.complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) space

overview.tagline: Precompute running totals so any range sum becomes a single subtraction.
whenToUse: You answer many range-sum queries over a fixed array.
You need a subarray that meets a sum condition, or a balance point.
Recomputing each range by looping would be O(n) per query.
The data doesn't change between queries.
overview.keyIdea: Build an array where prefix[i] is the sum of everything up to i. Then the sum of any range [l, r] is prefix[r] - prefix[l-1], which is O(1) instead of a loop. The same running-total idea finds balance points and target-sum subarrays in one pass.
overview.complexity: O(n) preprocessing, O(1) per range query

overview.tagline: Track the best subarray ending at each position to find the best overall in one pass.
whenToUse: You want the maximum (or minimum) sum or product of a contiguous subarray.
A brute force over all subarrays would be O(n^2).
The answer at position i can be built from the answer at i-1.
The array can include negative numbers.
overview.keyIdea: Walk left to right, keeping the best subarray that ends at the current cell: either extend the previous best or start fresh here. The largest running best is the answer, found in a single O(n) pass. For products, also track the min, since a negative can flip it into the new max.
overview.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space

overview.tagline: Use a last-in-first-out pile to track what you've seen but haven't resolved yet.
whenToUse: You process items in order but resolve them in reverse (matching, nesting).
You need the most recent unmatched or unresolved item, fast.
You're matching brackets, evaluating expressions, or finding a nearest greater/smaller element.
A monotonic stack can answer 'nearest bigger/smaller' in O(n).
overview.keyIdea: Push items as you go and pop when the top is resolved. Because the top is always the most recent item, a stack answers nesting and 'nearest previous' questions in one O(n) pass. Here the highlighted cells stand in for what's currently on the stack.
overview.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space

overview.tagline: Manipulate numbers and matrices directly, with careful index bookkeeping rather than a fancy data structure.
whenToUse: The problem is a 2-D grid you traverse, rotate, or mark in place.
It's digit or coordinate arithmetic, not a data-structure trick.
An in-place, O(1) extra-space rearrangement is expected.
Boundary-by-boundary or layer-by-layer movement solves it.
overview.keyIdea: Most of these come down to index discipline: track boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) or coordinates exactly and update them as you consume the grid. The challenge is the bookkeeping, not a clever structure.
overview.complexity: Typically O(m x n) time

overview.tagline: Process a hierarchy by recursing into the children and combining their answers.
whenToUse: The data is hierarchical: a root with left and right children.
A node's answer is built from its subtrees' answers.
You need a traversal: preorder, inorder, postorder, or level by level.
The problem says 'binary tree' or 'binary search tree'.
overview.keyIdea: Solve a node by asking the same question of its children first, then merging their results. Most tree problems are one short recursive function: handle the empty case, recurse left and right, and combine.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) time, O(h) space for recursion (h = height)

lessons.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
Kth Smallest Element in a BST
Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

overview.tagline: Walk a chain of nodes with a few pointers, rewiring next-arrows as you go.
whenToUse: The data is a chain of nodes, each pointing to the next.
You're reversing, merging, reordering, or detecting a cycle.
A couple of pointers (prev, curr, fast/slow) carry the whole solution.
You want O(1) extra space by re-pointing links instead of copying.
overview.keyIdea: Most list problems are a single pass with two or three pointers. The moves are always the same kit: save next, repoint a link, advance the pointers. The trick is doing it in the right order so you never lose the rest of the list.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) time, O(1) space

lessons.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

overview.tagline: Explore nodes and their connections with BFS or DFS, tracking what you've already visited.
whenToUse: The data is nodes joined by edges: a network, grid, or dependency.
You're finding connectivity, shortest paths, cycles, or an ordering.
You can reach an answer by spreading out from a start node.
A grid problem is really a graph where neighbors are adjacent cells.
overview.keyIdea: Visit nodes from a frontier, marking each visited so you never process it twice. BFS (a queue) explores level by level; DFS (recursion or a stack) goes deep first. The visited set is what keeps cycles from looping forever.
overview.complexity: Typically O(V + E) time and space

lessons.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph

overview.tagline: Trade memory for speed: a hash map turns repeated lookups into O(1) checks.
whenToUse: You repeatedly ask 'have I seen this value?' or 'where is it?'.
Counting frequencies, finding pairs, or de-duplicating.
A brute-force scan would be O(n^2) for the lookups.
Keys map naturally to values: number to index, char to count.
overview.keyIdea: Keep a map (or set) of what you've seen so each new element is one O(1) lookup plus one insert. Most array-and-hashing problems are a single pass that checks the map, then updates it.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) time, O(n) space

overview.tagline: Sort by an endpoint, then sweep once, deciding overlap from neighbors.
whenToUse: The input is ranges: time slots, segments, or [start, end] pairs.
You're merging, inserting, or counting overlaps.
After sorting, each interval only needs to look at the previous one.
You need the fewest rooms, removals, or merged ranges.
overview.keyIdea: Sort by start (sometimes end). Then a single left-to-right pass settles everything: two intervals overlap when the next start is at or before the current end. Sorting is what makes one comparison per interval enough.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n log n) time, dominated by the sort

lessons.title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query

overview.tagline: Build a candidate step by step; when a choice leads nowhere, undo it and try the next.
whenToUse: You must enumerate combinations, permutations, or subsets.
A solution is built by a sequence of choices.
You can prune: abandon a partial answer that can't possibly work.
The problem asks for 'all' valid arrangements, not just one.
overview.keyIdea: Explore a decision tree depth-first: make a choice, recurse, then undo it (backtrack) and try the next. Each leaf is one candidate. Pruning dead branches early is what keeps the exponential search tractable.
overview.complexity: Exponential in the worst case; pruning cuts it down

lessons.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

overview.tagline: Solve each subproblem once and store its answer, so larger cases reuse the smaller ones instead of recomputing them.
whenToUse: The answer for size n is built from answers to smaller sizes (n-1, n-2, ...).
A plain recursion would recompute the same subproblems over and over.
You're counting ways, or optimizing a min/max, over a 1-D sequence.
Each state depends on only a handful of earlier states.
overview.keyIdea: Define dp[i] as the answer up to position i, then fill the array left to right with a recurrence that combines a few earlier entries. Each entry is computed once, so an exponential search collapses to a single O(n) sweep.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) time, O(n) or O(1) space

overview.tagline: Take the locally best choice at each step and never look back. When that's provably enough, it beats searching every option.
whenToUse: A locally optimal pick at each step builds a global optimum.
You can argue you never need to undo an earlier choice.
A single scan or a sort exposes the best next move.
Searching all combinations would be exponential and unnecessary.
overview.keyIdea: Commit to the best immediate option, such as the farthest reach, the earliest finish or the biggest coin, and move on without backtracking. The real work is proving that this greedy choice can never be beaten by a more careful plan.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) or O(n log n) time, O(1) space

lessons.title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet

overview.tagline: Treat a number as a row of bits and compute with AND, OR, XOR, and shifts instead of arithmetic.
whenToUse: The problem is about individual bits, parity, or powers of two.
You want O(1) extra space and no auxiliary data structure.
XOR's self-cancelling property can isolate a unique or missing value.
Counting, toggling, or reversing bits is the core operation.
overview.keyIdea: Each bit is an independent on/off flag. AND masks bits, OR sets them, XOR toggles them (and cancels equal pairs), and shifts slide bits into view one at a time. Many counting and uniqueness problems collapse to a single pass of these tricks.
overview.complexity: Typically O(n) or O(1) time, O(1) space

overview.tagline: Fill a 2-D table where each cell builds on a few already-solved neighbours, turning an exponential search into a grid sweep.
whenToUse: The state needs two indices: two strings, or an item-and-capacity pair.
Each cell's answer depends on the cells above, to the left, or on the diagonal.
A plain recursion would recompute the same (i, j) subproblem many times.
You're counting paths or ways, or optimizing a min or max, over two dimensions.
overview.keyIdea: Define dp[i][j] over positions or prefixes in two dimensions, then fill the table row by row so each cell reuses neighbours that are already final. The recurrence, extend the diagonal on a match else take the best of top and left, is the whole algorithm.
overview.complexity: Typically O(m x n) time and space

lessons.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown

overview.tagline: Keep the largest or smallest item one step away by storing values in a heap, a tree that always surfaces its extreme at the root.
whenToUse: You repeatedly need the current min or max, not a full sort.
You want the k largest or k smallest, or a running median.
Items arrive over time and you must react to the extreme so far.
A full sort at every step would be too slow.
overview.keyIdea: A binary heap is a complete tree where every parent beats its children, so the extreme sits at the root. Push and pop sift one value up or down in O(log n), giving fast access to the min or max without sorting everything.
overview.complexity: O(log n) per push or pop, O(1) to peek the root

lessons.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
Kth Largest Element in an Array

overview.tagline: Store a set of words as a tree of shared prefixes, so lookups walk one letter at a time.
whenToUse: You store many strings and query by prefix.
You need fast insert and search keyed on characters.
Many words share leading letters you don't want to repeat.
Autocomplete, spell-check, or word-search style problems.
overview.keyIdea: Each edge is a letter and each root-to-node path spells a prefix, so words with a common start share one branch. Insert and search follow the path letter by letter in O(length), and a flag marks where a full word ends.
overview.complexity: O(L) per insert or search, where L is the word length

lessons.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

overview.tagline: The vocabulary of large systems: how to add capacity, keep data consistent, and stay up when parts fail.
whenToUse: You're sizing a system before designing it.
You need the tradeoffs behind scaling, caching, and replication.
You're preparing for a system-design interview.
You want the why behind the building blocks, not just their names.
overview.keyIdea: Most design decisions trace back to a few fundamentals: scale up versus out, where state lives, and what you trade away when something has to give, whether consistency, latency, or availability.

overview.tagline: The reusable components every large system is assembled from, and the tradeoffs baked into each.
whenToUse: You're choosing the pieces for a design, such as what stores data, spreads load, or moves messages.
You need a component's contract and failure modes, not just its name.
You're deciding between SQL and NoSQL, sync vs async, or a queue vs pub-sub.
You want to recognize the same blocks reused across every system.
overview.keyIdea: Most designs are a fresh arrangement of a small set of well-understood blocks: load balancers, databases, caches, queues. Learn each one's contract and tradeoffs once, and a design becomes a question of which blocks to combine and how to wire them.

overview.tagline: A repeatable way to drive a system-design interview from a blank page to a defended design.
whenToUse: You freeze at the start of a design question and don't know where to begin.
You jump to drawing boxes before pinning down requirements and scale.
You want a checklist that keeps availability, consistency, and scale from slipping.
You're structuring an answer under time pressure.
overview.keyIdea: Drive every design the same way: nail the requirements and the scale first, sketch a high-level design, then go deep where it matters and check it against the non-functional needs. Structure beats improvisation.

overview.tagline: End-to-end designs of real products, where the fundamentals and building blocks come together under the RESHADED method.
whenToUse: You want to see the building blocks assembled into a complete system.
You're practising the classic interview prompts, like design Twitter, YouTube or Uber.
You want to study the one hard tradeoff at the heart of each product.
You're rehearsing how to drive a design from requirements to evaluation.
overview.keyIdea: Every real system is the same handful of building blocks arranged to fit one dominant constraint, such as read-heavy fan-out, geospatial lookup, real-time delivery or exactly-once money. Find that constraint, design around it with the RESHADED steps, and the rest follows.
